question: The possibility of expanding the role of sustainable renewable fuels raises serious concerns regarding climate integrity, resource efficiency and investment certainty. Direct electrification remains the most efficient decarbonisation pathway for road transport.

A million hectares of photovoltaic panels could power 400 million electric vehicles (EVs) compared with the 32 million hectares currently used for biofuel production to fuel 130 million combustion engine vehicles. Europe’s 8 million EVs have already cut oil imports by 48 million barrels.
Alternative fuels are not cost-competitive: hydrotreated vegetable oil costs approximately 79 % more per 100 km than charging an EV; e-fuels are projected to reach EUR 7 per litre by 2030.

Recent analysis shows that a biofuel loophole in the Car CO2 Regulation would raise total EU demand to between two and nine times the sustainably available supply, putting it in direct competition with the aviation and maritime sectors, where no mature alternatives exist.

The current EU biofuel mix delivers only 20–40% life cycle CO2 savings, and certification fraud, including mislabelling of virgin palm oil as waste-based feedstock, risks erasing even those gains. Finally, unlike EVs, combustion engines emit local air pollutants which, according to the European Environment Agency, cause hundreds of thousands of premature deaths each year in the EU.

How does the Commission assess the climate, social and industrial risks of slowing direct electrification in order to accommodate alternatives that are insufficient, unscalable, more expensive and more polluting?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.7.2026) The Commission’s proposal amending Regulation (EU) 2019/6311 maintains a strong market signal for zero-emission vehicles, since vehicle electrification is the most efficient pathway to decarbonisation, energy security and independence, and it is the direction in which global markets are moving.

This supports continued investment by the EU industrial value chains in the transition and safeguards their competitiveness. At the same time, the proposal enhances technological neutrality by providing manufacturers with more flexibility to achieve their targets.

The contribution of renewable fuels is capped and limited to advanced and wastebased biofuels and renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO) that meet greenhouse gas and sustainability criteria, while other biofuel types, which would raise sustainability and food-competition concerns, are not incentivised, in line with the Renewable Energy Directive2.

The impact assessment3 accompanying the proposal provides a comprehensive analysis of the environmental, economic and social impacts of the options considered regarding the role of sustainable renewable fuels.

While acknowledging the benefits for the renewable fuels sector, it highlights the need for including appropriate safeguards to avoid that any shift away from electrification would lead to higher emissions, more energy consumption and an increased total cost of vehicle ownership for citizens.

This is also to avoid the risk that the limited availability of advanced biofuels and RFNBO hampers the decarbonisation of sectors without technological alternatives, such as aviation and maritime, and the achievement of the climate objectives set out in the European Climate Law.
1 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulation (EU) 2019/631

as regards CO2 emission performance standards for new light duty vehicles and vehicle labelling and repealing Directive 1999/94/EC, COM/2025/995 final. 2 http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/2413/oj. 3 SWD(2025) 1058 final.
